title: El Niño raises a conditional inflation risk for 2027
bank: Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco
summary: A weather cycle can lift prices in two distinct waves. Molly Ardren, Tobin Graf and Brigitte Roth Tran estimate that the 2026 El Niño lifted the US personal consumption expenditures price index about 0.3 percentage point above its counterfactual between April and July. Their historical estimates suggest that much of this first increase should unwind by the end of 2026. The larger risk comes later. A switch to La Niña could put prices roughly one percentage point higher over the course of 2027. When the authors account separately for the following year’s weather and remove that switch, the model implies essentially no further net price effect in 2027. A forecast of next year’s inflation therefore depends on a second weather development that was still unresolved at publication.

The analysis follows episodes from May, using NOAA’s Relative Oceanic Niño Index. Its three-month moving average must reach at least 0.5 for five consecutive months for the observations to qualify as an El Niño. A single peak reading would miss how long an episode lasts. The authors instead measure its cumulative strength over a 12-month period beginning in May, then use local projections to trace the subsequent paths of prices and payrolls. For the current episode they combine the index readings already in hand with NOAA’s median forecast and scale the historical responses in proportion to that magnitude. Some of the weather observations defining this particular shock were therefore forecasts when the estimates appeared.

The figure data show why the timing matters. July’s estimated price-level effect is 0.30 percentage point, with a 68% band from 0.13 to 0.48. By the following January, the point estimate is only 0.06 and the band spans −0.27 to 0.40. At the final plotted horizon, November of the second year, the estimate is 0.97, with a much wider band of 0.07 to 1.88. Each figure compares the price index with its estimated path in the absence of the episode. Reading successive figures as contributions to monthly inflation would count the same accumulated change more than once. The authors attribute the first summer’s pressure to core services, energy and food. In the second wave they single out core services and food. The figure workbook provides the headline path, while the component results are described in the text.

Payrolls follow a different timetable. The estimated employment response stays close to zero through much of the first year, with considerable uncertainty. It rises in the second year and remains positive in the authors’ analysis even when they account for whether a La Niña follows. The final plotted payroll response is about 1.94 percentage points, with a 68% band from 0.72 to 3.17. The authors also report a later improvement in unemployment, although they do not plot it. A joint rise in payrolls and prices in this particular scenario could therefore arise from weather and its international spillovers. Attributing it entirely to stronger domestic spending would require separate evidence.

The possible transmission mechanisms differ across regions and industries. A warmer northern winter can reduce heating demand and extend the time available for outdoor work. More rain in the South can interrupt construction and flooding can create demand for repairs. Weather disturbances overseas can also affect the US through traded goods and supply chains. The national impulse responses combine these channels. Even their direction can depend on intensity because rainfall that benefits production at moderate levels can cause losses beyond a flooding threshold.

The historical sample, which begins in the 1950s, contains 22 El Niño episodes and only four classed as very strong. NOAA’s projected current episode exceeds the historical sample in strength. The extrapolation assumes proportional effects beyond that range. Its confidence bands describe sampling uncertainty around the historical estimates and cannot cover every disaster outcome, error in the weather forecast, or change in households’ and firms’ capacity to adapt. Longer weather-warning lead times may help firms prepare, while deeper international supply relationships may amplify some overseas disruptions. The paper identifies a weather-contingent distribution of risks around a forecast. It supplies neither the probability of the following year’s La Niña nor a prescription for the policy rate.

questions.question: How much of the second-year price risk survives without a transition to La Niña?
questions.detail: Compare the response conditional on the following year’s index across episodes that turn to La Niña and those that persist or dissipate. Report the number and strength of episodes in each group. Track the meteorological forecast for the transition separately from revisions to the economic response conditional on it. Those are distinct reasons for revising an inflation projection.

questions.question: Can the four very strong historical episodes support a linear extrapolation?
questions.detail: Re-estimate the price and payroll responses after omitting each very strong episode in turn. Compare the resulting range with the published 68% bands and with estimates that permit responses to flatten or accelerate at high intensity. Sparse observations in the upper tail would justify reporting scenarios even if estimates near the middle of the historical sample look stable.

questions.question: Which evidence could distinguish domestic weather effects from overseas spillovers?
questions.detail: The letter points to heating, outdoor work, food and core services. Compare regions with different precipitation and temperature exposure, then track imported products or inputs by exposure of their source regions. Match labor and price responses at the same forecast horizons. A difference across US regions could identify a local channel even if a nationwide imported-price response were common to them all.

limitation: The published paths are model-implied differences from a counterfactual. The 2027 price result depends on the next weather regime and the current episode’s projected intensity lies beyond the historical sample.
